title: The kind sacrifice
hookLine: a king's great sacrifice with no animal killed: gifts to farmers, traders and workers
carry: let the animals drink cool water
last: WHERE ONE IS, THE OTHER IS.

lines: SEVEN HUNDRED OF EACH, TIED TO POSTS.
cards: Seven hundred bulls. Seven hundred bullocks, seven hundred heifers, seven hundred goats, seven hundred rams. All tied to posts in a village called Khanumata, waiting.
The brahmin Kutadanta is preparing a great sacrifice, the kind that was performed for prosperity and blessing in his world.
He wants it done perfectly, and he's heard that the Buddha knows the ancient way of performing a sacrifice, with its three modes and its sixteen requisites. So he goes to ask.

teach.b: The Buddha answers with a story. Long ago a rich king, Mahavijita, wanted to offer a great sacrifice, and asked his chaplain how. First, said the chaplain, look at your country.
It's full of bandits. Villages are raided, roads aren't safe. Raising taxes now would be wrong.
And don't think you can end this with executions and prisons; it won't work. Instead: to those who farm and keep cattle, give seed and feed. To those in trade, give capital.
To those who serve the state, give food and fair wages. The king did. The bandits disappeared, because people were busy with their work.
The text says people played with their children on their laps, and lived with their doors open. Only then came the sacrifice itself. No bulls were killed, no goats, no chickens, no pigs.

No trees were cut for posts, no grass was cut. No servant was made to work by threats or in tears; whoever wanted to help, helped, and whoever didn't, didn't. It was made with ghee, oil, butter, curds, honey and molasses.
The Pali word is yañña: sacrifice, offering. The story keeps the word and changes what it means. A sacrifice becomes a gift to the whole country, then simply giving, then virtue, then the path.
He frees the animals, seven hundred of each. Let them eat green grass, he says, and drink cool water, and may a cool breeze blow on them.

how: Buddhists across traditions practice dana, generosity, as a central offering: giving food and support to monastics and to people in need, and in many places releasing animals as an act of merit.

o: a tax paid to the king
a herd kept for a temple

games.q: the kind sacrifice: tap the pairs.
p: the brahmin with animals tied to posts
the king in the Buddha's story

s: the chaplain advises ending banditry with harsh punishments
he says punishment won't end it, and advises seed, capital and fair wages instead.
in the king's sacrifice, no animals were killed and no trees were cut
it was made with ghee, oil, butter, curds, honey and molasses.
Kutadanta frees the animals at the end
let them eat green grass, drink cool water, and feel a cool breeze.

games.q: you're King Mahavijita's chaplain. the king wants a great sacrifice, but the country is full of bandits. what do you advise first?
o: give seed to farmers, capital to traders and wages to officials.
raise taxes to pay for soldiers.
games.why: the chaplain says force won't end it. support people's work, and the bandits disappear, the treasury fills, and people live with their doors open.

practice: Think of one thing you were going to buy this week that you don't really need, and picture what that money or time could be as a gift: seed for someone's work, a meal, a fair tip, a donation.
Not out of guilt; just let the picture of the gift sit beside the picture of the purchase, and breathe with both.

wordCard.voice: Yañña. Sacrifice remade: no blood spilled, gifts given to farmers, traders and workers, and the animals set free.

orig.note: Pali yañña (Sanskrit yajña): sacrifice, offering. the word kept, its meaning changed in DN 5.

carryVoice: Your line: let the animals drink cool water. The old word stays, and what it means is remade. Until tomorrow.
